title: Your Flush Rides Downhill for Miles #shorts
summary: Most sewage moves by gravity: a 4-6 inch house lateral slopes to the street and joins a bigger sewer main (City of Madison); lift stations pump it up where the land climbs. New York City has more than 6,000 miles of sewer pipe and 95 pumping stations.
sources: New York City has 14 Wastewater Resource Recovery Facilities that together treat 1.3 billion gallons of wastewater daily; more than 6,000 miles of sewer pipes; 95 pumping stations (NYC DEP, Wastewater Resource Recovery Facilities): https://www.nyc.gov/site/dep/water/wastewater-treatment-plants.page

A sanitary sewer lateral runs from a building and slopes downward towards the street, typically 4, 5 or 6 inches in diameter for a single-family home; public sewer mains range from 8 to 36 inches in diameter; gravity moves most wastewater; lift stations pump wastewater to a gravity sewer where gravity alone won't work (City of Madison Engineering, How the Sanitary Sewer Works): https://www.cityofmadison.com/engineering/sanitary-sewer/education/how-the-sanitary-sewer-works

The sewer lateral connects the plumbing fixtures of a building (toilets, sinks, showers) to the sewer main (San Francisco Public Utilities Commission, How to take care of your sewer lateral): https://www.sfpuc.gov/about-us/news/how-take-care-your-sewer-lateral

scenes.narration: Your flush rides downhill. New York has over {6,000|six thousand} miles of sewer pipe.
It leaves home in a lateral, {4–6 in|four to six inches} wide, sloping to the street.
Then it joins a bigger pipe: the sewer main.
Where the land climbs, lift stations pump it up. New York has {95|ninety-five}.
Then gravity takes over again. So yes:
